summary:
Solar System Footprints is an interactive, free-roam 3D web experience that lets students explore the Solar System and discover the hardware humanity has left on other worlds. Users fly between the Sun, the planets and the Moon, click on any body, and find 23 pieces of NASA hardware, from the Apollo landing sites to Curiosity, Perseverance and the Voyager probes. Each one shows where it is, what its mission was, how it advanced scientific research, and includes an interactive 3D model.

It addresses abandoned but no forgotten by turning NASA mission information and open 3D resources into an engaging, explorable learning tool, making complex space missions easy to understand for non-experts.

It matters because many children and young people use technology every day but rarely see that someone designed, built and sent it to another world. By making real space hardware tangible and fun to explore, the project aims to spark curiosity about engineering, hardware and science, inspiring the next generation of space explorers.
details:
What it does and how it works
Solar System Footprints is a full-screen 3D model of the Solar System that users explore freely: rotate, zoom, pan and fly to any planet or moon with one click. Clicking a body opens a panel with its scientific data and the NASA hardware located there. Hardware with known coordinates appears as markers on the surface (for example, the six Apollo landing sites on the Moon, or Curiosity and Perseverance on Mars). For each of the 23 pieces of hardware, users can read its mission objective, its contribution to scientific research, its dates and its status, and open a page with an interactive 3D viewer. Mission data is stored in a structured data file, and a Three.js engine places each marker from its latitude and longitude on real planetary textures. The viewer loads the official NASA 3D model when available and a clearly labeled representative model otherwise.

Benefits
It turns static mission facts into an exploratory experience. It needs no installation or account, runs in any modern browser, and is free, so it can be used in classrooms with basic computers. It links each machine to what science learned from it, showing why the hardware mattered.

Expected impact
We want children and teenagers to see space technology as something people design and build, and to get curious about engineering, hardware and science. Teachers can use it as a visual resource, and the structure is easy to grow with more missions, languages and activities.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules); Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D scenes; Git and GitHub. An earlier prototype used PHP/Laravel and MySQL. Development was done on a standard personal computer, with no special hardware. Resources: NASA 3D Resources and NASA Science mission pages; Solar System Scope planetary textures (CC BY 4.0). Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code and text drafting, as disclosed in the SI field.

Creativity
Instead of a list of missions, we turned the Solar System into a map of “footprints”: real places where human-made machines still sit. Users can virtually visit the landing sites, follow the Moon around Earth, and inspect each machine in 3D. The focus on the hardware itself, and on what it taught us, is meant to inspire future engineers.

Factors we considered
Accuracy: facts, dates and coordinates were based on NASA mission information, and approximate data is labeled as such. Accessibility: browser-only, no sign-up, responsive layout, lightweight textures with a fallback when files are missing. Transparency: models that are not official are labeled as illustrative, and the planet scale is artistic so every world fits on screen. Licensing: all resources are credited (NASA media guidelines, CC BY 4.0), no NASA logos are used and the site states it is not affiliated with NASA. Safety and privacy: no personal data is collected, and no images of minors appear. Scalability: the data-driven design lets us add more hardware and missions easily.
